openers.tradable-permits-and-carbon-markets: Since 2005, every ton of carbon dioxide released by a covered European power plant or factory has needed a permit. That rule is the heart of {{ref:nature-pol-253}}: a government caps total emissions, issues permits, and lets polluters buy and sell them. Trading is meant to make cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost. This chapter follows the idea from theory to working markets in Europe and China, and weighs it against a {{ref:nature-pol-081}}, which fixes the price instead of the amount. It also hears the critics, who call carbon trading ineffective, unfair or open to abuse, and who warn that cuts in one country can raise emissions in another.

nature-pol-253.title: Emissions trading: a cap on pollution, a market in permits
nature-pol-253.text: What if the right to pollute were something a firm had to buy? Emissions trading, also called cap and trade, rests on that idea. A government caps the total amount of a pollutant that may be released and issues permits up to that cap. Each polluter must hold permits equal to its emissions. One that wants to emit more must buy permits from others willing to sell. In effect the buyer pays a charge for polluting, while the seller is rewarded for cutting its emissions. A {{ref:nature-found-031}}, a cost dumped on others, so acquires a price. The goal is to meet a set emissions target at the lowest cost. Unlike {{ref:nature-pol-147}}, which tells each firm what to do, trading lets firms decide how to meet the target. Some schemes let participants bank allowances for later periods, so they can cut emissions when it is most efficient. Usually the government lowers the overall limit over time towards a national reduction target. The approach is used for carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, and for sulfur dioxide and other pollutants. Does it work? A 2024 meta-analysis pooled 80 evaluations across 21 carbon-pricing systems. It found average emission cuts of about 5–21%, or around 4–15% after correcting for {{ref:nature-econ-241}}.

nature-pol-239.title: Carbon pricing: charging for the harm of greenhouse gases
nature-pol-239.text: Burning coal, oil or gas releases greenhouse gases, and no market charges for the harm they do. That makes the emissions a negative {{ref:nature-found-031}}, and carbon pricing is the standard remedy. It is a government policy that puts a money cost on {{ref:nature-eco-163}}, so that polluters burn less fossil fuel. The price usually takes one of two forms: a {{ref:nature-pol-081}}, or an emissions trading scheme in which firms must buy allowances to emit. Many economists consider it the most economically efficient way to cut emissions, because it fixes the unpriced external cost at its source, in the spirit of a {{ref:nature-pol-088}}. In 2025 carbon pricing covered 28% of global greenhouse gas emissions, and in 2020 it raised $53B in revenue. Of 21 schemes evaluated, at least 17 reduced emissions, by between 5% and 21%. A 2020 study found that carbon prices have not harmed economic growth in wealthy industrialized democracies. The weak point is the level of the price. About one third of schemes charge less than $10 per tonne of carbon dioxide ($10/tCO2), and most less than $40. Only Sweden and Switzerland exceed $100/tCO2. The IPCC says prices of $135–$5500 per tonne in 2030 and $245–$13,000 in 2050 would be needed to stay below the 1.5°C limit.

nature-pol-244.title: Carbon markets: trading the right to emit greenhouse gases
nature-pol-244.text: In 2023 carbon trading worldwide was worth a record 881 billion euros, and about 87% of it sat in the European Union's scheme. Carbon emission trading is {{ref:nature-pol-253}} applied to carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. A total limit on all participants' emissions sets the price. A polluter emitting more than its quota must buy the right from emitters with fewer emissions. In economic terms, the scheme creates property rights to the atmosphere, a global {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, to deal with an externality that crosses borders. Compliance is checked by comparing each emitter's actual emissions with the permits it surrenders. Countries use these markets to meet their pledges under the {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, with schemes running in China, the European Union and elsewhere. Prices vary widely. In September 2021 allowances cost €7 per tonne in China's national scheme and €63 per tonne in the EU's. The markets share two weaknesses. Their caps are usually not matched to the total emissions allowed if warming is to stay within 1.5 °C or 2 °C. And oversupply can push allowance prices too low to matter.

nature-pol-252.title: Carbon leakage: cuts at home, emissions abroad
nature-pol-252.text: Regulating emissions in one place can push them to places with less regulation. This is carbon leakage. It happens when climate policy raises local costs, so production moves to countries with laxer rules while demand stays the same. It can also run through fuel markets: lower demand cuts fuel prices, and countries without a carbon price use more. The leakage rate divides the rise in emissions outside the acting countries by the cut inside them. A rate above 100% would mean domestic action actually increased global emissions. Estimates for action under the {{ref:nature-clim-056}} ranged from 5 to 20%, but were seen as very uncertain. There is no consensus on how large leakage is in the long run. The EU gives free allowances to sectors at high risk, such as aluminum, ranked by trade intensity times emission intensity. Yet firm-level evidence found its trading scheme cut regulated manufacturers' CO₂ emissions by 14–16% with no observed leakage.

nature-pol-270.title: China's national carbon market: the largest of its kind
nature-pol-270.text: China proposed a carbon tax in 2010 but never passed it. Instead it set up an emissions trading scheme in February 2021, which began operating that year. Seven pilot markets came first, starting in Shenzhen on June 18, 2013, with compliance rates over 96%. The national scheme began with power plants and covers 40% of China's emissions, which is 15% of world emissions. No scheme of its kind is larger. Unusually, it caps {{ref:nature-clim-264}}, the emissions per unit of output, rather than the total. In July 2021 permits were handed out free and traded at around RMB 50 per tonne, roughly half the EU price. Studies find it cut carbon emissions by up to 18.2% and power sector emissions by 13% in 2013-2020. It also delivered about a third of China's air pollution health benefits. Some researchers found it can reduce GDP or hold back innovation. By 2027 it is expected to cover all major industrial emitters and move to an absolute cap for stable sectors.

nature-pol-254.title: Why permit trading puts the cheapest cuts first
nature-pol-254.text: Trading permits makes pollution cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost. The logic runs through each firm's books. A polluter compares the permit price with its {{ref:nature-clim-245}}: the extra cost of cutting one more unit of pollution, a kind of {{ref:nature-econ-347}}. Then it chooses to buy or sell permits, install cleaner technology or cut output. In theory this spreads reductions efficiently among polluters and lowers compliance costs compared with command-and-control rules. It is a version of the equi-marginal principle, which economists use to find the most efficient decision. In the mathematics of the least-cost target, the {{ref:nature-econ-455}} plays the role of the market permit price. The idea has a famous ancestor. Coase (1960) argued that social costs could be handled by negotiating property rights, assuming perfect markets and equal bargaining power ({{ref:nature-econ-629}}).

nature-pol-245.title: Free or auctioned: how permits are handed out
nature-pol-245.text: Once a government decides how many permits to issue, it must decide who gets them. There are two routes. Under free allocation, existing emitters receive permits and the government earns no carbon revenue. Under auctioning, it sells them and receives their full value on average. Either way the permits are equally scarce, so they sell at the same market price. The difference lies in who keeps the money. Emitters generally profit from permits given to them free, while paying for permits reduces their profits. Advance notice or a gradual introduction keeps the one-time cost of a new carbon price small.

nature-pol-272.title: The EU Emissions Trading System: Europe's carbon market
nature-pol-272.text: The European Union Emissions Trading System began in 2005 as the world's first large greenhouse gas trading scheme. Each allowance lets its holder emit 1 ton of CO2. It operates in 30 countries: the 27 EU states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway. As of 2026 it covers around 40% of the EU's emissions, and its cap should reach zero by 2039. Phase I issued too many permits, and this over-allocation drove the carbon price to zero in 2007. Between 2005 and 2023, emissions from covered power plants and factories fell by 47%. A 2023 study found it cut emissions by 10% between 2005 and 2012, with no significant effect on profits or employment. Fraud has struck too: hackers stole 28 to 30 million euros of allowances in 2011, and VAT fraud cost Germany about €850 million. Critics say over-allocation, windfall profits and price volatility mean it has failed its goals. Proponents call Phase I a learning phase and point to measured cuts.

nature-pol-249.title: The case against carbon trading
nature-pol-249.text: Supporters see carbon trading as an efficient climate tool. Critics call it ineffective, unjust and open to manipulation, and the argument is far from settled. The first objection is scale. Climate change, critics argue, needs more radical, systemic cuts in fossil fuel use than pollution trading can deliver. The second is direction. The market picks the easiest short-term carbon savings, which may differ from the steps needed to reduce climate change. The third is fairness. Carbon trading has been called a form of colonialism that lets rich countries keep consuming while claiming savings abroad. Then there is abuse. Some companies in China and India produced greenhouse gases artificially in order to earn credits for destroying them. Schemes have also been criticized for creating speculative markets through financial derivatives ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}), and for changes linked to money laundering.

nature-pol-240.title: Tax or cap: two ways to price carbon
nature-pol-240.text: A {{ref:nature-pol-081}} fixes the price of each tonne emitted and lets the amount adjust. Emissions trading does the reverse: it fixes the total amount emitted and lets the price move. Economists disagree over which is better. A tax is generally favored for its simplicity and price stability. It is also easier to enforce broadly: British Columbia enacted and implemented its carbon tax in five months. A cap can in principle hold emissions to a fixed remaining total. Most cap-and-trade programs lower the cap by a fixed percentage each year, guaranteeing that emissions decline. Permits therefore suit cases where certainty about emissions is needed. Prices under a cap are more volatile, though. That makes them riskier for investors, consumers and governments that auction permits. Both tools can be bent by politics. Industries may lobby their way out of a tax, while freely handed-out permits can invite corrupt behavior. On paper the two are close cousins. Both are efficient, and if permits are auctioned they have the same social cost and effect on profits. A last dispute concerns other climate policies. Some economists say a cap stops measures such as renewable energy support from cutting emissions further; others say only an enforced cap guarantees cuts ({{ref:nature-pol-242}}).

nature-pol-243.title: Internal carbon pricing: companies that charge themselves
nature-pol-243.text: As of 2024, 1,753 companies in 56 countries reported through the Carbon Disclosure Project that they put a price on their own greenhouse gas emissions. Internal carbon pricing is voluntary and comes on top of any price a government imposes. It works like a {{ref:nature-pol-088}} inside the firm, making fossil fuel use more expensive. Tools include internal emissions trading, proxy prices, carbon fees, implicit prices and hybrids of these. Proxy pricing, used by about two-thirds of reporting companies, writes a set carbon price into investment decisions without any actual payment. Companies often base their price on the {{ref:nature-clim-241}} or on the cost of the last cut needed to reach a target. An analysis of 500 firms reporting from 2011 to 2018 linked adoption to a significant fall in emissions per unit of revenue and per employee. Some researchers worry it can serve as {{ref:nature-nbs-075}}, deterring governments from stricter carbon rules.

nature-pol-275.title: Kyoto's flexible mechanisms: cutting emissions where it costs least
nature-pol-275.text: Cutting emissions costs different amounts in different places, but it benefits the atmosphere equally wherever it happens. That idea underlies the three flexible mechanisms of the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}: emissions trading, the {{ref:nature-mkt-104}} and {{ref:nature-pol-277}}. Each lets countries meet emission targets more cheaply by acting in other countries. The protocol required Annex I countries, the developed nations with targets, to cut emissions on average 5.2% below 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012. International emissions trading let parties buy Kyoto units from other countries to help meet their targets. The main argument for flexibility is cost-effectiveness, which keeps fairness separate from the efficiency of cutting emissions cheaply. Negotiators disagreed over whether that was wise. Critics feared rich countries would avoid domestic cuts and take up all the cheap reductions in developing countries. Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the {{ref:nature-clim-074}} are their successor.

nature-pol-262.title: The Acid Rain Program: America's first cap and trade
nature-pol-262.text: A US power plant that emitted a ton of sulfur dioxide beyond its allowances paid a fine of $2,000. That rule enforced the Acid Rain Program, the first cap-and-trade emissions program in the United States. Run by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), it cut sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides, the gases that cause {{ref:nature-pol-046}}. Title IV of the 1990 amendments to the {{ref:nature-pol-153}} set a falling cap on SO2, aiming to bring emissions to 50% of 1980 levels. In 2007 total SO2 emissions were 8.9 million tons, reaching the long-term goal ahead of the 2010 deadline. Its expected yearly cost by 2010, $1 billion to $2 billion, was only one fourth of the first prediction. A 2021 study found lasting air quality gains, cutting mortality risk by 5% over 10 years. The EPA, industry and economists call it a success, and it became a model for later greenhouse gas schemes. Skeptical environmentalists argue the cuts came from broader trends and other regulation. They note it cut SO2 by 40%, while conventional regulation in the European Union achieved more than 70%.

nature-pol-261.title: Europe's carbon charge at the border
nature-pol-261.text: Since 2026, firms bringing steel or cement into the European Union have had to pay for the carbon released in making it. The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM, is a {{ref:nature-pol-265}} on carbon-intensive imports. Its main aim is to stop {{ref:nature-pol-252}} by charging imports the same carbon price that EU producers pay under the EU ETS. Importers must buy CBAM certificates, priced in line with ETS allowances, to cover the emissions embedded in their goods. It covers aluminum, cement, electricity, fertilizers, hydrogen and iron and steel, with reporting from October 2023. Free ETS allowances in these sectors will be phased out by 2034. It may push other countries to price carbon: Brazil, Indonesia, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia and Serbia are doing so partly because of it. Some see it as the start of a {{ref:nature-clim-078}} of the kind proposed by {{ref:nature-hist-050}}. Critics are less impressed. An Asian Development Bank report says it will cut emissions only a little while harming imports to the EU. Questions also remain over its fit with {{ref:nature-pol-007}} rules and its effect on least developed countries.

nature-pol-277.title: Joint Implementation: emission projects between rich countries
nature-pol-277.text: Joint Implementation is a mechanism of the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. Under it, one developed (Annex I) country invests in an emission-cutting project in another and counts the cuts towards its own target. Projects earn credits ({{ref:nature-pol-271}}), each equal to one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. These come out of the host country's own pool of units, so the total among Annex I parties does not change. Because hosts also have emission commitments, it raised fewer concerns about spurious reductions than the {{ref:nature-mkt-104}}. Russia accounted for about two-thirds of projected savings, expected to total around 300 million units by 2012.

nature-pol-258.title: Baseline and credit: rewards for beating your own past
nature-pol-258.text: Not every trading scheme starts with a cap. In a baseline-and-credit scheme, polluters earn credits, or offsets, by cutting emissions below a baseline, often their own historical emissions. Polluters that face a regulatory limit can then buy those credits. Programs usually require {{ref:nature-mkt-144}}: the cuts must go beyond what existing rules already demand. That test is hard to define and monitor. Some companies deliberately raised their emissions in order to be paid to remove them.

nature-pol-255.title: From computer models to carbon markets
nature-pol-255.text: Emissions trading began as a computer result. Simulation studies of air pollution costs between 1967 and 1970 found that a least-cost solution was dramatically cheaper than conventional ways of cutting pollution. The 1977 Clean Air Act took up an offset mechanism: a firm could emit more if it paid another firm to cut the same pollutant. The first cap-and-trade system was the US {{ref:nature-pol-262}} under the 1990 Clean Air Act, announced as a paradigm shift in {{ref:nature-pol-018}}. From US clean air policy, the approach then spread to the European Union and to global climate policy.

nature-pol-259.title: Linking carbon markets across borders
nature-pol-259.text: California and Québec linked their cap-and-trade systems in 2014, and the EU's scheme has linked with Switzerland's. Linking means each system recognizes the other's allowances for compliance. The result is a larger carbon market, which can lower compliance costs, raise liquidity, the ease of finding a buyer or seller, and stabilize prices. Some scholars see linking as a bottom-up starting point for international climate policy, built from existing national and regional schemes.

nature-pol-281.title: Measure, report, verify: keeping a carbon market honest
nature-pol-281.text: A permit market is only as good as its numbers. Monitoring, reporting and verification are the checks that make it credible: emissions are measured or calculated, reported, then verified by government or third-party auditors. Some emissions are measured by sensors in chimneys, but many activities rely on calculations instead. Acid Rain Program plants had to monitor SO2 and NOx continuously and send data to the EPA daily. Polluters exceeding their allowances face fines and sanctions. The worries are the cost of checking and the risk of facilities lying. For voluntary credits, robust independent third-party validation and verification is one of the {{ref:nature-hist-034}}.

nature-pol-257.title: The safety valve: a cap with a price limit
nature-pol-257.text: A safety valve is a hybrid of a cap and a tax. Emitters can buy permits on the market, or from the government at a set trigger price, which holds the permit price below a maximum. Some designs instead hold it above a minimum. A trigger price set high enough, or a permit supply small enough, lets the system mimic a pure quantity or pure price instrument ({{ref:nature-pol-256}}). Each limit has a cost. A price ceiling removes the certainty of a fixed emissions limit. A price floor gives certainty for investment in cutting emissions, which matters when cuts are urgent.

nature-pol-247.title: Auctioning permits: making polluters pay up front
nature-pol-247.text: Businesses tend to oppose auctioning emission permits. Economists almost uniformly recommend it. Under auctioning, firms buy their permits at auction and the government receives their value. That revenue can fund low-carbon investment and cuts in distortionary taxes, the kind that discourage useful work and investment. Auctioning can also be more efficient and fairer than free allocation. And it removes the perverse incentive created by {{ref:nature-pol-246}}.

nature-pol-250.title: Carbon trading and the neighbors of polluters
nature-pol-250.text: Carbon trading can move money from richer, higher-emitting countries to poorer, lower-emitting ones for climate action. That is its promise as a tool of {{ref:nature-gov-162}}. The problem starts at the factory gate. Schemes cap only greenhouse gases, so a factory can buy permits instead of cutting its local air pollution. Low-income and minority communities living near emitters therefore keep facing an exposure gap. The sources record both sides: trading can advance that cause, yet it has also been linked to environmental injustice near emitters.

nature-pol-251.title: Toward a single global carbon market
nature-pol-251.text: In 2023 carbon markets worldwide were worth $948.75 billion, a figure expected to reach 2.68 trillion dollars by 2028. A truly worldwide market in emission allowances is still a proposal, though the {{ref:nature-clim-074}} provides a legal basis for one. At COP 30, the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets formed with a plan for a global cap near current emissions, falling to net zero by 2050. Such a market could speed emission cuts seven-fold in participating countries, while raising $200 billion per year for clean energy and social programs.
